chapters.title: גְּלִינְדָה הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הַטּוֹבָה מְמַלֵּאת אֶת מִשְׁאַלְתָּהּ שֶׁל דּוֹרוֹתִי
chapters.orig_title: Glinda The Good Witch Grants Dorothy’s Wish

s.line: Before they went to see Glinda, however, they were taken to a room of the Castle,
s.note: הוּבְלוּ = "they were led, taken". It is the hof'al (passive) of hif'il הוֹבִיל (to lead): הַשּׁוֹמֵר הוֹבִיל אוֹתָם → הֵם הוּבְלוּ. You will meet the noun in the news: הוֹבָלָה = transport, haulage.

s.line: where Dorothy washed her face and combed her hair,
s.note: With your own body parts, Hebrew usually says "the face, the hair" where English says "her face, her hair": <t>רָחַצְתִּי אֶת הַיָּדַיִם</t> = I washed my hands. The comb is <t>מַסְרֵק</t>, from the same root as <t>סֵרֵק</t>.

s.line: and the Lion shook the dust out of his mane,
and the Scarecrow patted himself into his best shape,
and the Woodman polished his tin and oiled his joints.
s.note: שִׁמֵּן (pi'el) = to oil, made straight from the noun שֶׁמֶן (oil), as in his כַּד שֶׁמֶן. Hebrew often builds a pi'el verb from a noun like this. לִטֵּשׁ = to polish; keep it in mind for this chapter.

s.line: When they were all quite presentable they followed the soldier girl into a big room where the Witch Glinda sat upon a throne of rubies.
s.note: יִצּוּגִי = "presentable, respectable", an everyday modern word: תִּלְבַּשׁ מַשֶּׁהוּ יִצּוּגִי (wear something decent). It comes from יִצֵּג (to represent). אֹדֶם is "redness" and also "lipstick"; אֶבֶן אֹדֶם is a ruby. הָלַךְ אַחֲרֵי = followed.

s.line: She was both beautiful and young to their eyes.
s.note: בְּעֵינֵי X = "in X's eyes, in X's opinion": בְּעֵינַי זֶה סֶרֶט מְצֻיָּן (to me it's an excellent film). גַּם … וְגַם … = "both … and …".

s.line: Her hair was a rich red in color and fell in flowing ringlets over her shoulders.
s.note: גּוֹלֵשׁ = sliding, flowing down. גָּלַשׁ is also the verb for surfing, skiing and browsing: גְּלִישָׁה בָּאִינְטֶרְנֵט (surfing the net). A תַּלְתַּל is a curl; מְתֻלְתָּל = curly.

s.line: Her dress was pure white but her eyes were blue,

w: בְּטוּב לֵב|kindly|~lit. with goodness of heart
s.line: and they looked kindly upon the little girl.
s.note: הֵן: עֵינַיִם is feminine, so "they" is הֵן and the verb has a feminine plural subject. טוּב לֵב = kindness; טוֹב לֵב = kind-hearted.

s.line: “What can I do for you, my child?” she asked.
s.note: יַלְדָּתִי = "my child", a fixed address form with the possessive ending, like בִּתִּי (my daughter). In ordinary talk you would hear מָה אֲנִי יְכוֹלָה לַעֲשׂוֹת בִּשְׁבִילֵךְ? in any shop or office.

s.line: Dorothy told the Witch all her story:

w: לְאֶרֶץ אוֹז|to the Land of Oz
חֲבֵרֶיהָ לַדֶּרֶךְ|her companions|~lit. her friends for the road
s.line: how the cyclone had brought her to the Land of Oz, how she had found her companions, and of the wonderful adventures they had met with.
s.note: חֲבֵרִים לַדֶּרֶךְ = companions, fellow travelers; it is also used figuratively for people who share a cause. עָבַר + an experience = "went through": עָבַרְתִּי יוֹם קָשֶׁה (I had a hard day).

s.line: “My greatest wish now,” she added, “is to get back to Kansas,
s.note: הִיא here is the linking "is" between a subject and its description; it agrees with מִשְׁאָלָה (feminine). הוֹסִיף = to add, hif'il of י־ס־ף; נוֹסָף = additional.

s.line: for Aunt Em will surely think something dreadful has happened to me,
and that will make her put on mourning;
s.note: גָּרַם לְX + infinitive = "made X do something": הַסֶּרֶט גָּרַם לִי לִבְכּוֹת (the film made me cry). בִּגְדֵי אֵבֶל = mourning clothes, black clothes that cost money. That is Dorothy's worry.

s.line: and unless the crops are better this year than they were last,

w: לְהַרְשׁוֹת לְעַצְמוֹ|to afford|~idiom: lit. to permit himself
s.line: I am sure Uncle Henry cannot afford it.”
s.note: לְהַרְשׁוֹת לְעַצְמוֹ = "to afford", lit. "to allow oneself": אֲנִי לֹא יָכוֹל לְהַרְשׁוֹת לְעַצְמִי מְכוֹנִית חֲדָשָׁה. "Unless" is most simply אִם … לֹא; the formal word is אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן. הַשָּׁנָה שֶׁעָבְרָה = last year.

s.line: Glinda leaned forward and kissed the sweet, upturned face of the loving little girl.
s.note: נִשֵּׁק (kissed) is pi'el, even though the נִ at the start makes it look like a nif'al; the root itself begins with נ. Present: מְנַשֵּׁק. מוּרָם (raised) is the hof'al participle of הֵרִים (to lift).

s.line: “Bless your dear heart,” she said, “I am sure I can tell you of a way to get back to Kansas.”
s.note: מְתוּקָה שֶׁלִּי ("my sweet one") is a warm everyday endearment, the natural modern match for "bless your dear heart". To a boy: מָתוֹק שֶׁלִּי.

s.line: Then she added, “But, if I do, you must give me the Golden Cap.”
s.note: תִּצְטָרְכִי "you will need, will have to" is the future of הִצְטָרֵךְ, the hitpa'el of צ־ר־ך: after צ the ת of the prefix moves inside and becomes ט. Since צָרִיךְ has no future of its own, this form fills in: תִּצְטָרֵךְ לְחַכּוֹת = you'll have to wait.

s.line: “Willingly!” exclaimed Dorothy;

w: אֵין לִי|I have no|~lit. there is not to me
s.line: “indeed, it is of no use to me now,
s.note: מִמֵּילָא = "anyway, in any case", very common in speech: מִמֵּילָא לֹא רָצִיתִי לָלֶכֶת (I didn't want to go anyway). אֵין לִי צֹרֶךְ בְּ… = I have no need of …; צָרִיךְ and הִצְטָרֵךְ share its root.

s.line: and when you have it you can command the Winged Monkeys three times.”
s.note: אֶצְלֵךְ = "at your place, with you": הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת אֶצְלִי (I've got the keys). תּוּכְלִי is the irregular future of יָכוֹל: אוּכַל, תּוּכַל, יוּכַל. צִוָּה עַל = to order, command; מִצְוָה comes from the same root.

s.line: “And I think I shall need their service just those three times,” answered Glinda, smiling.
s.note: הִזְדַּקֵּק לְ… = to need, to require, a step up in register from צָרִיךְ. It is hitpa'el of ז־ק־ק, and after ז the ת becomes ד (compare תִּצְטָרְכִי above). The nif'al participle נִזְקָק means "needy": מִשְׁפָּחוֹת נִזְקָקוֹת.

s.line: Dorothy then gave her the Golden Cap,
and the Witch said to the Scarecrow, “What will you do when Dorothy has left us?”
s.note: אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ + future for something that hasn't happened yet: אַחֲרֵי שֶׁתִּגְמֹר, תִּתְקַשֵּׁר (after you finish, call). English uses the present ("has left"), Hebrew the future. Same with כְּשֶׁ.

s.line: “I will return to the Emerald City,” he replied, “for Oz has made me its ruler and the people like me.
s.note: מִנָּה לְ… (pi'el) = to appoint as …; the noun is מִנּוּי (appointment; also a subscription). In pa'al, מָנָה means "to count". שֶׁלָּהּ is feminine because עִיר is feminine.

s.line: The only thing that worries me is how to cross the hill of the Hammer-Heads.”
s.note: A binyan pair: pa'al דָּאַג = to worry (אַל תִּדְאַג = don't worry), hif'il הִדְאִיג = to cause worry: זֶה מַדְאִיג אוֹתִי (it worries me). מַצָּב מַדְאִיג (a worrying situation) is common in the news.

s.line: “By means of the Golden Cap I shall command the Winged Monkeys to carry you to the gates of the Emerald City,” said Glinda,
s.note: לָשֵׂאת is the infinitive of נָשָׂא (to carry), whose first letter נ drops: future יִשָּׂא. נָשָׂא also appears in נָשָׂא אִשָּׁה (married a woman) and נוֹשֵׂא (a topic, subject).

s.line: “for it would be a shame to deprive the people of so wonderful a ruler.”
s.note: שָׁלַל מִX = to take away from X, to deny X: שָׁלְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ אֶת הָרִשְׁיוֹן (they revoked his license). It also means "to rule out": אֲנִי לֹא שׁוֹלֵל אֶת זֶה. חֲבָל you know as "what a pity".

s.line: “Am I really wonderful?” asked the Scarecrow.

w: יוֹצֵא דֹּפֶן|unusual|~idiom: lit. going out of the side wall
s.line: “You are unusual,” replied Glinda.
s.note: יוֹצֵא דֹּפֶן = "out of the ordinary", for better or worse: כִּשָּׁרוֹן יוֹצֵא דֹּפֶן (an exceptional talent). Glinda's answer is carefully polite, which is the joke.

w: מָה יִהְיֶה אִתְּךָ|what will become of you|~idiom: lit. what will be with you
s.line: Turning to the Tin Woodman, she asked, “What will become of you when Dorothy leaves this country?”
s.note: מָה יִהְיֶה אִתְּךָ? = "what will become of you?", often a half-despairing "what am I going to do with you?". פָּנָה אֶל = turned to, addressed; פְּנִיָּה = an appeal, a request (to an office).

s.line: He leaned on his axe and thought a moment.
s.note: נִשְׁעַן עַל = to lean on, a nif'al with active meaning. Its relative מִשְׁעֶנֶת is the back of a chair or a walking stick.

s.line: Then he said, “The Winkies were very kind to me,
and wanted me to rule over them after the Wicked Witch died.
s.note: רָצָה שֶׁ… + future: "wanted (someone) to …". Hebrew can't say "wanted me to rule"; it says "wanted that I will rule". שָׁלַט בְּ… = to rule, to control (הוּא שׁוֹלֵט בְּאַנְגְּלִית = he has a good command of English). שַׁלִּיט is from this root, and so is שַׁלָּט, the TV remote.

s.line: I am fond of the Winkies,

w: לְאֶרֶץ הַמַּעֲרָב|to the Country of the West
s.line: and if I could get back again to the Country of the West, I should like nothing better than to rule over them forever.”
s.note: מְחַבֵּב = to like, be fond of (pi'el of ח־ב־ב), milder than אוֹהֵב; חָבִיב = nice, pleasant. מִלִּ + infinitive = "than to …": אֵין דָּבָר טוֹב יוֹתֵר מִלִּישֹׁן (there's nothing better than sleeping).

s.line: “My second command to the Winged Monkeys,” said Glinda “will be that they carry you safely to the land of the Winkies.
s.note: פְּקֻדָּה = an order, a command, also used for a computer command. בְּשָׁלוֹם = "safely, in one piece": הִגַּעְנוּ הַבַּיְתָה בְּשָׁלוֹם (we got home safely).

s.line: Your brain may not be so large to look at as those of the Scarecrow,
but you are really brighter than he is—when you are well polished—and I am sure you will rule the Winkies wisely and well.”
s.note: Baum's pun works in Hebrew too: מַבְרִיק means both "shiny" and "brilliant, very clever". From בָּרָק (lightning). מְלֻטָּשׁ is the pu'al (passive) participle of לִטֵּשׁ: polished → "was polished". יַהֲלוֹם מְלֻטָּשׁ = a cut diamond.

w: מָה יִהְיֶה אִתְּךָ|what will become of you|~idiom
s.line: Then the Witch looked at the big, shaggy Lion and asked, “When Dorothy has returned to her own home, what will become of you?”
“Over the hill of the Hammer-Heads,” he answered, “lies a grand old forest,
s.note: מֵעֵבֶר לְ… = beyond, on the other side of; also figuratively: מֵעֵבֶר לַצִּפִּיּוֹת (beyond expectations). מְפֹאָר = splendid, a pu'al participle (lit. "made glorious"), from פְּאֵר (glory). נִמְצָא = "is located", an active-meaning nif'al.

s.line: and all the beasts that live there have made me their King.
s.note: חַיּוֹת שֶׁחַיּוֹת: the same word twice. חַיּוֹת = animals, and חַיּוֹת = "live" (feminine plural present of חַי). הִכְתִּיר = to crown, from כֶּתֶר (crown). Sports news uses it: הוּכְתַּר כְּאַלּוּף (was crowned champion).

w: הָיִיתִי מְבַלֶּה|I would spend|pi'el ptc · ב־ל־ה
s.line: If I could only get back to this forest, I would pass my life very happily there.”
s.note: אִם הָיִיתִי …, הָיִיתִי … = "if I could …, I would …". Modern Hebrew uses הָיָה + participle in both halves of an unreal condition. בִּלָּה = to spend time; לְבַלּוֹת on its own = to have a good time, go out: בִּלִּינוּ בְּתֵל אָבִיב.

s.line: “My third command to the Winged Monkeys,” said Glinda, “shall be to carry you to your forest.

w: כְּשֶׁאֲנַצֵּל|when I will have used|pi'el · נ־צ־ל
s.line: Then, having used up the powers of the Golden Cap, I shall give it to the King of the Monkeys,
s.note: נִצֵּל (pi'el) = to make use of, to exploit: לְנַצֵּל הִזְדַּמְּנוּת (to seize an opportunity). Unpointed ניצל can also be the nif'al נִצַּל = "was saved" (הוּא נִצַּל מֵהַשְּׂרֵפָה), the same root in a different binyan. Context decides.

w: מֵעַכְשָׁיו וּלְתָמִיד|from now on forever|~fixed phrase
s.line: that he and his band may thereafter be free for evermore.”
s.note: כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = "so that": דַּבֵּר לְאַט כְּדֵי שֶׁאָבִין (speak slowly so I'll understand). לַהֲקָה = a band, troupe or flock: לַהֲקַת רוֹק (a rock band), לַהֲקַת צִפּוֹרִים (a flock of birds).

w: מִכָּל הַלֵּב|wholeheartedly|~idiom: lit. from all the heart
s.line: The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman and the Lion now thanked the Good Witch earnestly for her kindness;
s.note: הוֹדָה לְ… עַל … = to thank someone for something; תּוֹדָה is from the same root. With בְּ it means "to admit": הוּא הוֹדָה בָּאַשְׁמָה (he admitted the charge), a phrase you'll see in court news.

s.line: and Dorothy exclaimed:
“You are certainly as good as you are beautiful!
s.note: בְּהֶחְלֵט = "definitely, certainly", and on its own a firm "absolutely!" in answer to a question. הֶחְלִיט = to decide, same root.

s.line: But you have not yet told me how to get back to Kansas.”
“Your Silver Shoes will carry you over the desert,” replied Glinda.

w: הָיִית יוֹדַעַת|you had known|pa'al ptc · י־ד־ע
הָיִית יְכוֹלָה|you could have|pa'al ptc · י־כ־ל
s.line: “If you had known their power you could have gone back to your Aunt Em the very first day you came to this country.”
s.note: אִם הָיִית יוֹדַעַת …, הָיִית יְכוֹלָה …: one pattern serves both "if you knew" and "if you had known". Context tells you it's about the past. שֶׁלָּהֶן is feminine plural because נַעֲלַיִם is feminine.

w: הָיִיתִי מְקַבֵּל|I would have gotten|pi'el ptc · ק־ב־ל
s.line: “But then I should not have had my wonderful brains!” cried the Scarecrow.

w: הָיִיתִי מְבַלֶּה|I would have spent|pi'el ptc · ב־ל־ה
s.line: “I might have passed my whole life in the farmer’s cornfield.”

w: הָיִיתִי מְקַבֵּל|would have gotten|pi'el ptc · ק־ב־ל
s.line: “And I should not have had my lovely heart,” said the Tin Woodman.

w: הָיִיתִי עוֹמֵד|I would have stood|pa'al ptc · ע־מ־ד
s.line: “I might have stood and rusted in the forest till the end of the world.”
s.note: הֶחְלִיד (hif'il) = to rust, to become rusty, from חֲלוּדָה (rust). The pa'ul participle חָלוּד = rusty. Many hif'il verbs describe "becoming" something: הֶאֱדִים (turned red), הֶחְוִיר (went pale).

w: הָיִיתִי נִשְׁאָר|would have remained|nif'al ptc · שׁ־א־ר
s.line: “And I should have lived a coward forever,” declared the Lion,
s.note: הִכְרִיז = to declare, announce; הַכְרָזָה is an announcement, and כָּרוֹז a town crier. In the news: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל … (the government announced …).

w: הָיְתָה אוֹמֶרֶת|would have said|pa'al ptc · א־מ־ר
s.line: “and no beast in all the forest would have had a good word to say to me.”

w: שֶׁהָיִיתִי לְעֵזֶר|that I was of help|~idiom: lit. I was for help
s.line: “This is all true,” said Dorothy, “and I am glad I was of use to these good friends.
s.note: הָיָה לְעֵזֶר = "was of help, was useful": אִם אוּכַל לִהְיוֹת לְעֵזֶר, תַּגִּיד (if I can be of help, say so). הָיָה לְ… often means "became, served as".

s.line: But now that each of them has had what he most desired, and each is happy in having a kingdom to rule besides,
s.note: בְּנוֹסָף = "in addition, besides", from הוֹסִיף (to add). בְּנוֹסָף לְ… = in addition to …. מַה שֶּׁ… = "what, the thing that": זֶה מַה שֶּׁרָצִיתִי (that's what I wanted).

w: שֶׁהָיִיתִי רוֹצָה|that I would like|pa'al ptc · ר־צ־ה
s.line: I think I should like to go back to Kansas.”
s.note: הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה = "I would like", the polite form of אֲנִי רוֹצָה. You'll hear it when ordering: הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה קָפֶה, בְּבַקָּשָׁה.

s.line: “The Silver Shoes,” said the Good Witch, “have wonderful powers.
And one of the most curious things about them is that they can carry you to any place in the world in three steps,
s.note: בְּיוֹתֵר after an adjective = "the most": הַמַּפְלִיאִים בְּיוֹתֵר (the most amazing). It is a little more formal than הֲכִי before the adjective. שְׁלוֹשָׁה צְעָדִים: צַעַד is masculine, so the number takes ה.

w: כְּהֶרֶף עַיִן|in the blink of an eye|~idiom
s.line: and each step will be made in the wink of an eye.
s.note: יֵעָשֶׂה = "will be done, made", the nif'al (passive) of עָשָׂה: past נַעֲשָׂה. כְּהֶרֶף עַיִן ("like a blink of the eye") = in an instant, still the normal phrase.

w: זֶה בָּזֶה|against each other|~lit. this in this
s.line: All you have to do is to knock the heels together three times and command the shoes to carry you wherever you wish to go.”
s.note: הִקִּישׁ = to knock, tap; today it also means "to type, key in": הַקֵּשׁ אֶת הַסִּסְמָה (enter the password). זֶה בָּזֶה = "against each other, together" (masculine; with feminine nouns זוֹ בְּזוֹ).

s.line: “If that is so,” said the child joyfully, “I will ask them to carry me back to Kansas at once.”
s.note: A pa'al/hif'il pair: חָזַר = to come back; הֶחְזִיר = to bring or give back: תַּחְזִיר לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר (give me back the book). בִּקֵּשׁ מִ… = to ask (someone) for something, with מִ.

s.line: She threw her arms around the Lion’s neck and kissed him,
s.note: כָּרַךְ = to wrap, to wind around. From the same root: כְּרִיךְ (a sandwich, lit. something wrapped) and כֶּרֶךְ (a volume of a book). כָּרוּךְ בְּ… = involves, entails: זֶה כָּרוּךְ בְּהוֹצָאוֹת (it involves expenses).

s.line: patting his big head tenderly.
s.note: Don't mix up לִטֵּף (to stroke, pet) with לִטֵּשׁ (to polish) from the start of the chapter: only the last letter differs. לְלַטֵּף כֶּלֶב = to pet a dog.

s.line: Then she kissed the Tin Woodman, who was weeping in a way most dangerous to his joints.
s.note: מְסֻכָּן (dangerous) is, like מְאֻשָּׁר, a pu'al participle in form; סַכָּנָה = danger. בְּצוּרָה + adjective is a very common way to make an adverb: בְּצוּרָה מְסֻכֶּנֶת = dangerously.

s.line: But she hugged the soft, stuffed body of the Scarecrow in her arms instead of kissing his painted face,
s.note: מְמֻלָּא = stuffed, filled (pu'al of מִלֵּא, to fill). On a menu: פִּלְפְּלִים מְמֻלָּאִים (stuffed peppers). Note the word order: the object אֶת הַגּוּף … comes first, for contrast with the kisses.

s.line: and found she was crying herself at this sorrowful parting from her loving comrades.
s.note: פְּרֵדָה = parting, separation; the verb is נִפְרַד מִ… (to part from, say goodbye to). בּוֹכָה stays in the present after גִּלְּתָה שֶׁ, as in other reported thoughts.

s.line: Glinda the Good stepped down from her ruby throne to give the little girl a good-bye kiss,
s.note: נְשִׁיקַת פְּרֵדָה = a goodbye kiss, a construct pair: נְשִׁיקָה → נְשִׁיקַת. In the same way: מְסִבַּת פְּרֵדָה (a farewell party).

s.line: and Dorothy thanked her for all the kindness she had shown to her friends and herself.
s.note: עָשָׂה חֶסֶד עִם … = "did a kindness to …", a set phrase: תַּעֲשֶׂה לִי חֶסֶד = do me a favor (often sarcastic: "oh, give me a break"). עִמָּהּ = אִתָּהּ, with her.

s.line: Dorothy now took Toto up solemnly in her arms,
s.note: בַּחֲגִיגִיּוּת = solemnly, ceremonially, from חַג (holiday) and חֲגִיגָה (celebration). הֵרִים (hif'il) = to lift; its hof'al participle מוּרָם (raised) appeared earlier in this chapter.

w: אָמְרָה שָׁלוֹם|she said goodbye|~idiom: lit. said peace
s.line: and having said one last good-bye she clapped the heels of her shoes together three times, saying:
s.note: אָמַר שָׁלוֹם works for both hello and goodbye, since שָׁלוֹם is both greetings. A more specific goodbye is נִפְרַד: הִיא נִפְרְדָה מֵהֶם (she said goodbye to them).

s.line: “Take me home to Aunt Em!”
s.note: קְחוּ is the plural imperative of לָקַח; she is talking to the shoes. Old Hebrew had a separate feminine plural form, קַחְנָה, but modern Hebrew uses קְחוּ for everyone. הַבַּיְתָה = homeward: the ending ָה means "toward", as in צָפוֹנָה (northward).

s.line: Instantly she was whirling through the air,
s.note: הִסְתַּחְרֵר = to whirl, spin, a hitpa'el of a four-letter root. It also means "to feel dizzy": הָרֹאשׁ שֶׁלִּי מִסְתַּחְרֵר (my head is spinning); סְחַרְחֹרֶת = dizziness. After ס the ת of the prefix swaps places with it.

s.line: so swiftly that all she could see or feel was the wind whistling past her ears.
s.note: שָׁרַק = to whistle; שְׁרִיקָה = a whistle (also the referee's: שְׁרִיקַת הַסִּיּוּם, the final whistle). רוּחַ is feminine here, hence שֶׁשָּׁרְקָה. כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ… = "so … that …".

s.line: The Silver Shoes took but three steps,
and then she stopped so suddenly that she rolled over upon the grass several times before she knew where she was.
s.note: נֶעֱצַר here is "came to a stop", an active-meaning nif'al of עָצַר (to stop something). In the news it is passive: הַחָשׁוּד נֶעֱצַר = the suspect was arrested. הִתְגַּלְגֵּל = to roll; גַּלְגַּל = wheel.

s.line: At length, however, she sat up and looked about her.
s.note: הִתְיַשֵּׁב = to sit down or sit up (from lying). It also means "to settle (in a place)", hence הִתְיַשְּׁבוּת = settlement.

w: אֱלֹהִים אַדִּירִים|good gracious|~idiom: lit. mighty God
s.line: “Good gracious!” she cried.
s.note: אֱלֹהִים אַדִּירִים! is a common exclamation of shock or amazement, like "good heavens!". It is everyday speech, not a prayer.

s.line: For she was sitting on the broad Kansas prairie,
and just before her was the new farmhouse Uncle Henry built after the cyclone had carried away the old one.
s.note: מוּל = opposite, facing; with endings מוּלִי, מוּלוֹ, מוּלָהּ. מַמָּשׁ = "really, right": מַמָּשׁ פֹּה (right here). בֵּית הַחַוָּה is a construct pair; the article goes on the second word only.

s.line: Uncle Henry was milking the cows in the barnyard,
s.note: Three words share the unpointed spelling חלב: חָלַב = he milked, חָלָב = milk, and חֵלֶב = animal fat. מֶשֶׁק = a farm, household, or economy: מֶשֶׁק בַּיִת (housekeeping), הַמֶּשֶׁק הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (the Israeli economy).

s.line: and Toto had jumped out of her arms and was running toward the barn, barking furiously.
s.note: רֶפֶת = a cowshed, dairy barn; a barn for hay is אָסָם. לְעֵבֶר = toward, a little more written than לְכִוּוּן. בְּטֵרוּף = madly, frantically (מְטֹרָף = crazy).

s.line: Dorothy stood up and found she was in her stocking-feet.
s.note: גַּרְבַּיִם = socks or stockings (singular גֶּרֶב). בִּלְבַד = "only", placed after the word it limits; a bit more formal than רַק before it.

s.line: For the Silver Shoes had fallen off in her flight through the air,
s.note: בְּמַהֲלַךְ = "during, in the course of", very common in news and everyday speech: בְּמַהֲלַךְ הַשָּׁבוּעַ (during the week). טִיסָה = a flight, as at the airport.

s.line: and were lost forever in the desert.
